weak.e: From Middle English waik, wayk, wayke, weik, weyk, borrowed from Old Norse veikr (“weak”), from Proto-Germanic *waikwaz (“weak, yielded, pliant, bendsome”), from *wīkwaną (“to cease, fold, yield; to retreat”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, turn, wind”), from *weh₁y- (“to plait, twist, weave, wind; to cover, enclose, wrap”).
weak.g: Lacking in force (usually strength) or ability.

weakness.e: From Middle English weyknesse, replacing earlier Middle English wocnesse, wakenes, wacnesse (“weakness”), from Old English wācnes (“weakness”). Equivalent to weak + -ness.

wealth.e: From Middle English welth, welthe (“happiness, prosperity”), from Old English *welþ, *welþu, from Proto-West Germanic *waliþu (“wealth”). Alternatively, possibly an alteration (due to similar words in -th: compare helth (“health”), derth (“dearth”)) of wele (“wealth, well-being, weal”), from Old English wela (“wealth, prosperity”).
wealth.g: Riches; a great amount of valuable assets or material possessions.

wealthy.e: From Middle English welthy, welþi, equivalent to wealth + -y.

wean.e: From Middle English wenen, from Old English wenian (“to accustom; habituate; train; prepare; make fit”), from Proto-West Germanic *wannjan, from Proto-Germanic *wanjaną (“to make wont; accustom”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive for; wish; love”). Related via PIE to wone, wont, and wonder, and perhaps win.
wean.g: To cease giving breast milk to an offspring; to accustom and reconcile (a child or young animal) to a want or deprivation of mother's milk;

weapon.e: From Middle English wepen, from Old English wǣpn, from Proto-West Germanic *wāpn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną (“weapon”), of unknown origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wēbnom.
weapon.g: An instrument of attack or defense in combat or hunting, e.g. most guns, missiles, or swords.

wear.e: From Middle English weren, from Old English werian (“to clothe, cover over; put on, wear, use; stock (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *waʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *wazjaną (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to dress, put on (clothes)”). Originally a weak verb (i.e.

From Middle English weren, werien, from Old English werian (“to guard, keep, defend; ward off, hinder, prevent, forbid; restrain; occupy, inhabit; dam up; discharge obligations on (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną (“to defend, protect, ward off”).
wear.g: To guard; watch; keep watch, especially from entry or invasion.

weariness.e: From Middle English werynes, werinesse, from Old English wēriġnes (“weariness”), equivalent to weary + -ness.

wearisome.e: From Middle English werisom, equivalent to weary + -some.

weary.e: From Middle English wery, weri, from Old English wēriġ (“weary”), from Proto-West Germanic *wōrīg, *wōrag (“weary”).
weary.g: Having the strength exhausted by toil or exertion; tired; fatigued.

weasel.e: From Middle English wesele, from Old English weosule, from Proto-West Germanic *wisulā, from Proto-Germanic *wisulǭ.
weasel.g: Any of the carnivorous mammals of the genera Mustela, Neogale, Poecilogale, and Lyncodon, having a slender body, a long tail and usually a l

weather.e: From Middle English weder, wedir, from Old English weder, from Proto-West Germanic *wedr, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰrom (=*we-dʰrom), from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). Other cognates include Sanskrit निर्वाण (nirvāṇa, “blown or put out, extinguished”).
weather.g: The short-term state of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, including the temperature, relative humidity, cloud cover, precipitatio

weave.e: From Middle English weven (“to weave”), from Old English wefan (“to weave”), from Proto-West Germanic *weban, from Proto-Germanic *webaną, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to weave, braid”).
weave.g: To form something by passing lengths or strands of material over and under one another.

weave.e: From Middle English weven (“to wander”); probably from Old Norse veifa (“move around, wave”), related to Latin vibrare.
weave.g: To move by turning and twisting.

weaver.e: From Middle English wevere, wever, from Old English *wefere, *wifre, *wæfre (“weaver”, in compounds), from Proto-West Germanic *webārī. By surface analysis, weave + -er.
weaver.g: A person who weaves; especially, one who weaves cloth for a living.

web.e: From Middle English web, webbe, from Old English webb, from Proto-West Germanic *wabi, from Proto-Germanic *wabją (“web”), from Proto-Germanic *webaną (“to weave”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to braid, weave”).
web.g: The silken structure which a spider builds using silk secreted from the spinnerets at the caudal tip of its abdomen; a spiderweb.

wedding.e: From Middle English wedding, weddynge, from Old English weddung (“betrothal, espousal”), equivalent to wed + -ing.
wedding.g: A marriage ceremony; a ritual officially celebrating the beginning of a marriage.

wedge.e: From Middle English wegge (“wedge”), from Old English weċġ (“wedge”), from Proto-West Germanic *wagi, from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz.
wedge.g: One of the simple machines; a piece of material, such as metal or wood, thick at one edge and tapered to a thin edge at the other for insert

wedge.e: From Wedgewood, surname of the person who occupied this position on the first list of 1828.
wedge.g: The person whose name stands lowest on the list of the classical tripos.

wedlock.e: From Middle English wedlok, wedlocke (“wedlock, marriage, matrimony”), from Old English wedlāc (“marriage vow, pledge, plighted troth, wedlock”). By surface analysis, wed + -lock.

week.e: From Middle English wyke, weke, from Old English wice, wucu (“week”), from Proto-West Germanic *wikā, from Proto-Germanic *wikǭ (“sequence; week”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyg-, *weyk- (“to bend, curve”).
week.g: Any period of seven consecutive days.

weep.e: From Middle English wepen, from Old English wēpan (“to weep, complain, bewail, mourn over, deplore”), from Proto-West Germanic *wōpijan, from Proto-Germanic *wōpijaną (“to weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂b- (“to call, cry, complain”).
weep.g: To cry; to shed tears, especially when accompanied with sobbing or other difficulty speaking, as an expression of emotion such as sadness or
A lapwing; wipe, especially, a northern lapwing (Vanellus vanellus).

weeping.g: Action of the verb to weep.

weigh.e: From Middle English weyen, from Old English wegan, from Proto-West Germanic *wegan, from Proto-Germanic *weganą (“to move, carry, weigh”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰeti, from *weǵʰ- (“to bring, transport”).
weigh.g: To determine the weight of an object.

weight.e: From Middle English weight, weiȝte, weght, wight, from Old English wiht, ġewiht (“weight”), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz ("weight"; compare *weganą (“to move”)), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to move; pull; draw; drive”). Equivalent to weigh + -t (abstract nominal suffix).
weight.g: The downwards force an object experiences due to gravity.

weighty.e: From Middle English weighti, weghti, wighti, equivalent to weight + -y.
weighty.g: Having a lot of weight; heavy.

welcome.e: From Middle English welcome, wolcume, wulcume, wilcume, from Old English wilcuma (“a wished-for guest”; compare also wilcume (“welcome!”, interjection)), from Proto-West Germanic *willjakwemō.
welcome.g: Whose arrival is a cause of joy; received with gladness; admitted willingly to the house, entertainment, or company.

welcoming.e: From Middle English welcomyng, equivalent to welcome + -ing.

welding.g: The action or process of welding:

welfare.e: From Middle English welefare, probably from the Old English phrase wel faran (“to fare well, get along successfully, prosper”) (cognate with Middle Dutch welvare (“welfare”), Middle Low German wolvare (“welfare”), Middle High German wolvar, wolfar (“welfare”)). Equivalent to well + fare.
welfare.g: Health, safety, happiness and prosperity; well-being in any respect.

well.e: From Middle English wel, wal, wol, wele, from Old English wel (“well, abundantly, very, very easily, very much, fully, quite, nearly”), from Proto-Germanic *wela, *wala (“well”, literally “as wished, as desired”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“wish, desire”).

From Middle English welle, from Old English wielle (“well”), from Proto-West Germanic *wallijā, from Proto-Germanic *wallijǭ (“well, swirl, wave”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn; wind; roll”).
well.g: A hole sunk into the ground as a source of water, oil, natural gas or other fluids.

well-built.g: Constructed in a pleasing or sound manner.

well-known.e: From Middle English well knowen. By surface analysis, well + known.
well-known.g: Familiar, famous, renowned, noted or widely known.

wellspring.e: From Middle English wellespring, from Old English wiellspring, wiellġespring (“spring, fount, fountain”), corresponding to well + spring.
wellspring.g: The source of water for a stream, spring or well; a fountainhead; a wellhead.

welt.e: From Middle English welten, from Old English weltan, wieltan, from Proto-Germanic *waltijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to turn; wind; twist”).

First use appears c. 1425, a shoemaker's term. Perhaps related to Middle English welten (“to overturn, roll over”), from Old Norse velta (“to roll”). Meaning "ridge on the skin from a wound" first recorded 1800.
welt.g: A ridge or lump on the skin, as caused by a blow or insect bite.

wen.e: From Middle English wen, wenne, from Old English wenn, wænn (“wen”), from Proto-Germanic *wanjaz.
wen.g: A cyst on the skin; a tumor or wart.
Obsolete form of wynn (“the letter ƿ”).

wench.e: The English word is cognate with Old High German wenken (“to waver; to give way, yield”), wankōn (“to totter”).
wench.g: A girl or young woman, especially a buxom or lively one.

went.e: Originally the simple past and past participle of wend, but now the past of go due to suppletion. While wend is akin to wind, compare typologically Russian смота́ться (smotátʹsja), сма́тываться (smátyvatʹsja), умота́ть (umotátʹ), ума́тывать (umátyvatʹ) (akin to мота́ть (motátʹ)).
went.g: A course; a way, a path; a journey.

west.e: From Middle English west, from Old English west, from Proto-West Germanic *westr (“western”), from Proto-Germanic *westrą (“west”), from Proto-Germanic *westraz (“west”), from Proto-Indo-European *wek⁽ʷ⁾speros (“evening”).
west.g: The direction opposite to that of the earth's rotation, specifically 270°.

western.e: From Middle English westerne, from Old English westerne, from Proto-Germanic *westrōnijaz. By surface analysis, west + -ern.
western.g: Of, facing, situated in, or related to the west.

westward.e: From Middle English westward, from Old English westweard.

wet.e: From Middle English wet (“wet, moistened”), wett, wette, past participle of Middle English weten (“to wet”), from Old English wǣtan (“to wet, moisten, water”), from Proto-West Germanic *wātijan, from Proto-Germanic *wētijaną (“to wet, make wet”), from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water, wet”) (also the source of water).
wet.g: Made up of liquid or moisture, usually (but not always) water.

go.e: From Middle English gon, goon, from Old English gān (“to go”), from Proto-West Germanic *gān, from Proto-Germanic *gāną (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave”). The inherited past tense form yode (compare Old English ēode) was replaced through suppletion in the 15th century by went, from Old English wendan (“to go, depart, wend”).
go.g: To move, either physically or in an abstract sense:

go.e: From Japanese 碁(ご) (go), shorter variant of Japanese 囲碁(いご) (igo), from Chinese 圍棋 /围棋 (wéiqí, literally “encirclement board game”).
go.g: A strategic board game, originally from China and today also popular in Japan and Korea, in which two players (black and white) attempt to c

be.e: From Middle English been (“to be”). Further etymology of be and its conjugated forms The various forms have three separate origins, which were mixed together at various times in the history of English. The forms beginning with b- come from Old English bēon (“to be, become”), from Proto-Germanic *beuną (“to be, exist, come to be, become”).
A variant of by which goes back to Middle English be (variant of Middle English bi).
be.g: Alternative form of by. Also found in compounds, especially oaths, e.g. begorra begad and bejesus.
